title: How to choose the right air compressor for your workshop
excerpt: Air delivery, pressure, tank size, belt or direct drive — the few numbers that decide which compressor will keep up with your tools.
html:
An air compressor that is too small runs non-stop, overheats and leaves your tools short of air. One that is too big costs more to buy and run. Getting it right comes down to a few numbers you can find in your tools’ manuals.

1. Start with the air your tools use

Every air tool lists how much air it needs, in litres per minute (l/min) or CFM. Add up the tools that will run at the same time, then add around 30% for hose leaks and wear.

  • Tools used in short bursts — nailers, impact wrenches, blow guns, tyre inflators — need less air than you might think.
  • Tools that run continuously — sanders, grinders, spray guns, sandblasters — need a compressor that can keep up all the time.

Compare your total with the compressor’s free air delivery (FAD), not its displacement. Displacement is what the pump moves in theory; FAD is the air you actually get, and it is noticeably lower on piston compressors.

2. Check the pressure

Most air tools are made to work at about 6.2 bar (90 psi). A compressor that reaches 8–10 bar keeps the tank above that while you work, so the tool doesn’t lose power as the tank empties.

3. Tank size: a buffer, not extra air

A bigger tank smooths out short, heavy demands and lets the motor rest between cycles. It does not increase how much air the pump makes. For continuous jobs, choose by FAD first and tank size second.

4. Direct drive or belt drive?

TypeBest for
Direct driveCompact and affordable. Good for occasional use, small workshops, tyre inflation and nailers.
Belt driveThe pump turns slower and runs cooler, so it lasts longer. Best for garages and workshops where air is needed all day.

5. Oil-lubricated or oil-free?

Oil-lubricated pumps are more durable — the usual choice for regular workshop use. Oil-free compressors are lighter and need less maintenance, which suits light or mobile work.

6. Match your power supply

Smaller compressors run on a normal single-phase socket. Larger workshop units usually need a three-phase supply. Check what you have on site before you order.

7. Look after it in the UAE heat

  • Install it in a shaded, well-ventilated place — heat is the main cause of early wear.
  • Drain the water from the tank every day; humid air leaves a lot of condensation.
  • Check the oil level and clean the air filter regularly, especially on dusty sites.

title: Non-sparking tools: what they are and when you need them
excerpt: Why oil & gas, marine and petrochemical sites use aluminium bronze and beryllium copper tools — and how to use them safely.
html:
On oil & gas sites, refineries, tank farms and ships, a single spark can ignite flammable gas, vapour or dust. Non-sparking tools are made to reduce that risk. Here is what they are, where they are used and what to keep in mind.

What makes a tool “non-sparking”?

Instead of hardened steel, these tools are made from copper alloys — mainly aluminium bronze and beryllium copper. If they strike or rub against a surface, any sparks they produce carry far less energy than steel sparks. The alloys are also non-magnetic and resist corrosion, which makes them useful in marine and chemical environments too.

Where are they used?

  • Oil & gas production, refineries and petrochemical plants
  • Fuel and chemical storage tanks, pipelines and pump stations
  • Ships, offshore platforms and shipyards
  • Paint shops, solvent stores and gas plants
  • Flour mills, grain stores and other places with explosive dust

Aluminium bronze or beryllium copper?

Aluminium bronzeBeryllium copper
Strength & hardnessGoodHigher — closer to steel tools
PriceMore affordableHigher
Typical choiceGeneral maintenance workHeavy-duty work and high torque

Common non-sparking tools

Spanners (open, ring and combination), adjustable and pipe wrenches, hammers and mallets, sockets, chisels, scrapers, pliers and screwdrivers. Many sites order complete kits so every crew has the same set.

Good to know

  • They are softer than steel. Use the right size, don’t extend handles with pipes and replace worn tools.
  • Keep them clean. Steel particles stuck to a tool can still spark — store them separately from steel tools.
  • Don’t grind or re-sharpen beryllium copper without proper dust controls; the dust is hazardous.
  • The work surface matters too. Striking rusty or hard steel can produce sparks from the steel itself.
  • Non-sparking tools are one part of safe work in hazardous areas — always follow your site’s permits, gas testing and safety rules.

title: Cordless or corded? Choosing power tools for site work
excerpt: When battery tools make sense, when a cable still wins, and how to look after batteries in the UAE heat.
html:
Cordless tools have taken over most job sites, but corded tools still have their place. Here is how to decide which is right for the work you do.

Why cordless

  • Freedom to move — no hunting for sockets or running extension leads across the site.
  • Safer sites — fewer trailing cables to trip over or damage.
  • One battery, many tools — drills, impact drivers, grinders, saws and lights share the same packs.

The big brands each have their own battery platform: DeWALT 18V XR and 54V FLEXVOLT, Makita 18V LXT and 40V XGT, Milwaukee M12 and M18, and Bosch 18V Professional. Batteries only fit tools from the same platform, so it pays to choose one and stay with it.

When corded is still the better choice

  • Work that runs for hours without a break — large 230 mm grinders, core drilling, wall chasing, mixing.
  • Fixed workshop setups, where a socket is always within reach.
  • Tight budgets — a corded tool costs less up front, with no batteries or charger to buy.

Brushless motors and battery size

Brushless tools turn more of the battery’s energy into work, so they run longer, stay cooler and need less maintenance. Battery capacity (Ah) decides runtime: a 2.0 Ah pack keeps a drill light, while grinders and circular saws work better on 5.0 Ah or bigger packs.

Quick guide

JobOur suggestion
Drilling, driving, fixing on siteCordless drill driver + impact driver
Occasional cutting and grindingCordless 115/125 mm grinder, brushless
All-day cutting of steel or concreteCorded 230 mm grinder or cut-off saw
Drilling concrete, light chisellingSDS-plus rotary hammer (cordless or corded)
Demolition and breakingCorded breaker, or a high-voltage cordless model

Battery care in the UAE heat

  • Don’t leave batteries in a parked car or in direct sun.
  • Let hot packs cool down before charging — most chargers pause until the battery is cool enough.
  • For long storage, keep batteries partly charged in a cool, dry place.
